sections.h2: What the Recorder of Deeds does
sections.html:
Property sales become public record here. Look for the Third Street section, first floor, inside the Beaver County Courthouse at 810 Third Street, Beaver; the phone is 724-770-4560. The counter keeps weekday hours of 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

Recording here began in 1800, and every record has since been digitized. The filing list is long: sheriff deeds, tax claim deeds, satisfactions, assignments, releases, restrictive covenants, leases, installment land contracts, Clean and Green filings and notary bonds, in addition to deeds and mortgages. Pennsylvania realty transfer tax is collected here too, with the local portion sent on to the municipality and school district.

A free Fraud Alert will notify you any time a deed or mortgage is recorded in your name. Since other people in the county may share that name, compare each alert with your own property before you react.

Beaver is the county seat, and Aliquippa is its largest city. An estimated 166,032 people lived here in 2025, in 79,845 housing units. Three quarters of homes (75.0%) are lived in by their owners and typically value $190,900. Estate sales and downsizing moves account for many listings.

Expect 2% of the value conveyed. The state keeps 1%, and local governments share the other 1% evenly between municipality and school district. That value may differ from the price you agreed on. Everything is collected when the deed is filed, and no deed is accepted before the tax is paid.

Taxing bodies are indifferent about who writes the check, which leaves it to your purchase agreement. Many contracts split it between buyer and seller, though the buyer is on the hook if the amount is questioned afterward. One check to the Recorder of Deeds can cover the fees and both taxes. Cash or check is all the office takes.

Transfer tax parts and copy charges

Deed recording fees changed December 1, 2025, with a new schedule that adds a $1 Criminal Justice Enhancement Account charge under Act 45 of 2025. Ask the office for today’s schedule before you plan your closing costs.

sections.h2: Statement of value and common level ratio
sections.html:
The statement of value is a two-copy state form. It either puts a value on the property or explains why the transfer is exempt. The office wants one when tax is unpaid or when the deed hides the real value, as with $1.00 of stated consideration. Investigators for the state may audit these forms later.

The form calls for the county’s common level ratio, set at 1.34 for documents accepted between July 1, 2026 and June 30, 2027. By 61 Pa. Code 91.02, acceptance is presumed to fall on the execution date written in the deed.

  • Exempt transfers run between spouses, from parent to child, grandparent to grandchild, among siblings, and between stepparent and stepchild.
  • Further exemptions cover particular situations; an attorney or the state Department of Revenue can advise.
  • If the state later decides the value was higher, or an exemption does not hold, the Department of Revenue mails a determination. You pay the added state and local tax plus interest to the state, and the Recorder then disburses the local share.

Walk it in or mail it. A visit takes roughly 10 to 15 minutes for review, receipt and scanning, and the stamped original comes back by mail within about a week. When a mailed package fails to return after two weeks, contact the Postal Service.

By mail, include a correctly sized check to the Recorder of Deeds and a stamped return envelope with enough postage. Short postage and lost returns are not the office’s responsibility, and cash should never go in the mail. You will probably not do this yourself, since the title company or closing attorney files the deed. Have that person tell you the filing date and forward the recorded copy.

  • Documents that touch more than one municipality need the local tax split clearly stated.
  • Subdivision plans must be 18 by 24 inches or 24 by 36 inches, original on linen or mylar, and no older than 90 days from governing body approval.
  • A military discharge can be recorded through the courthouse basement office that serves former service members, and the Recorder issues certified copies at no charge.

sections.h2: Looking up a deed or mortgage
sections.html:
Beaver County indexes by name, not by street address or tax parcel number. To find a deed or mortgage you need the name of the grantor, grantee, mortgagor or mortgagee and the approximate year. Parcel numbers come from the Assessment Office, so if you only have an address, start there.

Every document in the office is public except military discharge papers, which are impounded. Staff can answer general questions by phone but cannot run searches or give legal advice, so a title searcher or attorney handles anything deeper. To trace ownership backward, read the recital that follows the legal description, usually beginning with the word Being, and follow it through each prior deed toward 1800.

The county records deeds for land only, not buildings. Older deeds sometimes mention when a structure was built, but the Recorder does not keep construction records. Check with the municipality for those.

sections.h2: Selling with liens or an unreleased mortgage
sections.html:
Confirm that the payoff of your existing mortgage ends with a recorded satisfaction piece. The lender starts that step and may send you the forms. If it fails to file, you can bring or mail the original satisfaction piece to the Recorder with the fee and a stamped return envelope.

Before you list, pull your own name from the index and read what is recorded against it. Open mortgages, old easements and agreements show up there, and clearing a missing satisfaction is quicker before an offer than during the closing window.

  • Gather the last recorded deed and its recital.
  • Ask the Assessment Office for the parcel number.
  • Ask your lender for the recorded satisfaction on any paid-off loan.
  • Agree in writing who pays the 2% transfer tax.

sections.h2: Cash sales and the recording step
sections.html: When a buyer pays cash, the deed is recorded the same way and the same 2% tax applies. The difference is that no lender stands behind the closing, so there is no loan approval to wait on and no lender checklist to meet. Put the tax split in the contract, ask the closing agent for the filing date, and keep the recorded copy with your sale papers. If you suspect someone filed something against your property, use the Fraud Alert and check the index by name.

faqs.q: Who pays the realty transfer tax when a house sells in Beaver County?
faqs.a: The contract decides, and the county offices do not mind which side pays as long as the full amount is collected at recording. On most agreements the buyer and seller split it, but the new owner is responsible if the amount is questioned later.

faqs.q: What hours is the Beaver County Recorder of Deeds open?
faqs.a: The office is open 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., Monday through Friday, at 810 Third Street in Beaver. The phone number is 724-770-4560, and the office is on the first floor of the courthouse in the Third Street section.

faqs.q: Can I pay the recording fee and transfer tax with one check?
faqs.a: Yes. Recording fees plus the state and local taxes can all be on one check made payable to the Recorder of Deeds. The office accepts only cash or check, and you should not mail cash.

faqs.q: Does the Recorder search by address in Beaver County?
faqs.a: No. The indexes are by the names of grantor, grantee, mortgagor and mortgagee, grouped by year. Parcel numbers and addresses are handled by the Assessment Office.

faqs.q: How long does Beaver County take to return a recorded deed?
faqs.a: A walk-in filing is reviewed, receipted and scanned in about 10 to 15 minutes, and the recorded original is mailed back within about a week. If a mailed filing has not come back after two weeks, contact the Postal Service.
